transcript:
Header: 2026-04-20 16:00 UTC | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Avery Chen, Diego Morales, Priya Patel (Redwood) / Sarah Park, Ravi Kumar, Elaine Johnson, Matt O'Neil (Apex)

[00:00] Avery (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, we'll run through Optimize — quant profiles, INT8 and FP8, show some latency vs quality numbers, answer infra and security q's. Diego and Priya are here to do the deep bits.
[00:14] Sarah (Apex CTO): Thanks, Avery. We're mostly focused on the clinical summarization flow — P99 latency needs to be under 300ms for short notes, and quality can't degrade more than, like, 2% on Rouge/EM for our test set.
[00:28] Diego (Redwood SE): Got it. Quick show of hands — are you looking at Hosted first or Dedicated/Private right away?
[00:34] Ravi (ML Eng): We want to evaluate Hosted for speed of onboarding but think Dedicated for production because of data residency and keys. Also Elaine will want to see KMS/HSM support.
[00:45] Elaine (Security): Yep, SOC two and SSO/SAML + audit logs are musts. Also curious about model pinning and auditability for rollouts.
[00:54] Avery: Totally — we'll include the security pack. Quick agenda: high-level workflow, quantization primer, live charts (latency vs quality), and then Q&A + next steps.
[01:12] Priya (Product): I'll start with a short primer — quantization reduces precision to shrink model size and speed up kernels; INT8 is more aggressive, FP8 tends to preserve quality for certain layers. In practice FP8 sits between FP16 and INT8 on quality but often has lower speedup than INT8.
[01:35] Ravi: When you say "preserve quality" is that across generative and classification tasks? Our summarization is generative with longer contexts.
[01:42] Diego: Good question — FP8 tends to keep generation more stable, especially for long-range attention and KV cache behavior; INT8 can introduce occasional hallucinations or tokenization artifacts on longer sequences. But depends on the model and per-layer calibration.
[01:58] [02:05] Avery: We're going to pull up a benchmark we ran on Redwood-13B (note: model names are internal) — this was on a 48GB A100 equiv node with continuous batching.
[02:18] Diego: Here's a slide (link: https://redwood.example/optimize/benchmarks) — apologies if the link is clipped in transcript — the core takeaway: INT8 gave ~2.3x throughput and median latency drop ~45% for short prompts, but for 1k sequence the quality delta vs FP16 was 3–5% on our internal rouge metric. FP8 gave ~1.6x throughput and quality delta 0.8–1.2%.
[02:50] Sarah: That 3–5% for INT8 is higher than we can accept. How much of that is tunable via per-layer quant calibration or fallback?
[03:02] Diego: We do per-layer quant-profiling in Optimize — we generate a quant profile based on a calibration corpus (preferably your prompt set). We can do selective layer-quant or mixed-precision where critical layers stay in FP16. That typically recovers most of the delta.
[03:21] Ravi: Is that something the platform auto-suggests or do you need us to run a bigger calibration corpus?
[03:27] Priya: Optimize will suggest a profile given a sample corpus — it gives expected quality vs latency plots. But for production we prefer you to provide your representative prompts so the profile is tuned to the real workload.
[03:39] [04:05] Matt (Infra): What about KV cache behavior — does INT8 increase KV retrieval time or cause more misses?
[04:12] Diego: KV is mostly orthogonal; however INT8 can cause subtle distribution shifts in logits which affect caching for partial prefix matches — we've seen increased cache misses in some synthetic tests, but with continuous batching and prefix caching strategies Redwood's runtime mitigates most of that. We log cache hit rates per route so you can observe.
[04:33] Elaine: On the security side — we need to ensure quantization artifacts don't leak PII in a way that affects compliance. Any known issues?
[04:41] Avery: Good point — quantization shouldn't affect input privacy; models still operate on the same tokenization. The bigger risk is behavior change affecting hallucination that might surface sensitive info. We'll add that to the evals — Redwood Optimize ties quality regression alerts to your prompt set so you can flag regressions post-quantization.
[04:58] [06:00] Diego: Live demo: here are two runs of the same clinical note prompts — left column FP16 baseline, middle FP8, right INT8. You can see examples of truncated tokens on INT8 in longer outputs (example snippet shown). Note: transcription of slide text may be off, link: https://redwood.example/optimize/samples.
[06:23] Sarah: Can you quantify hallucination increase? We need numbers not just examples.
[06:28] Diego: Sure — in this benchmark on 5k prompts, hallucination-like divergence (our internal metric) increased from 0.9% at FP16 to 1.5% at FP8 and 2.7% at INT8. Again, with selective layer FP16 we got INT8 down to ~1.6%.
[06:45] Ravi: What's the expected cost delta? If INT8 is 2.3x throughput that's great but does that map linearly to $/token?
[06:53] Priya: Not perfectly linear — you save GPU time but also may need more overhead for calibration and potentially higher inference retries. For rough numbers: INT8 could drop inference cost ~30–45% vs FP16 depending on batch efficiency; FP8 ~15–25%. We'll produce a cost estimate based on your throughput numbers.
[07:14] [08:10] Avery: Let's talk SLOs and routing — you can route critical requests to FP16 or FP8 and lower-tier traffic to INT8, or use automated fallback if quality falls below a threshold. This gives an operational lever: keep low-latency path but maintain quality windows.
[08:35] Elaine: For auditability, we need model versioning and deterministic rollbacks. Is that supported?
[08:40] Diego: Yes — model pinning, rollouts, and automatic fallback are in Console. We also store per-request metadata (model version, quant profile id) in audit logs — retention configurable.
[08:53] Sarah: What's the impact on latency for cold-starts and caching when we use FP8/INT8?
[09:00] Diego: Cold-start overhead is slightly lower for quantized models due to reduced memory footprint but kernel warm-up characteristics vary; typical cold-start delta was 50–150ms in our tests depending on model size and hardware.
[09:15] [10:30] Ravi: We have a long-tail of sequence lengths; do you recommend stratified profiles?
[10:37] Priya: Yes — Optimize supports multiple profiles per model depending on sequence length buckets. For instance, short-seq profile uses aggressive INT8 + small batch, long-seq uses FP8 or mixed. We can auto-select at runtime based on request metadata.
[10:54] Matt: Any special infra to run FP8? Does it require specific drivers or cudnn versions?
[11:02] Diego: FP8 kernels are available on recent CUDA + cuBLAS/cudNN stacks; our private deployment has a compatibility matrix. We'll share exact versions. For Hosted it's handled by Redwood.
[11:18] [12:00] Avery: Quick slide with recommended checklist for Apex: 1) Provide prompt corpus; 2) Define quality/regression thresholds; 3) Choose pilot route (Hosted vs Dedicated); 4) Run 1k/10k prompt benchmark; 5) Review security pack.
[12:22] Sarah: Sounds good. For the pilot, do you need raw logs or just outputs? We have privacy concerns.
[12:30] Elaine: We prefer to keep PHI off any external logs; can Redwood ingest masked or synthetic prompts?
[12:36] Diego: Absolutely — masked or synthetic calibration corpora work for calibration. If you go Dedicated/Private, we can do full-calibration inside your VPC and keep logs on-prem.
[12:49] [14:00] Priya: Now showing latency vs quality chart for Apex-like prompts (note: numbers are illustrative) — x-axis latency (ms) y-axis quality delta vs FP16. FP8 cluster around 100–180ms with quality delta <1%, INT8 cluster 60–120ms with quality delta 1.5–4%.
[14:25] Ravi: Those INT8 latency numbers look great for short notes. The quality delta is still worrying. Can we do mixed-mode at runtime?
[14:31] Diego: Yes — runtime supports selective layer FP16 + INT8 hybrid and can flip per-request via headers or route rules. You can do A/B test traffic to measure user impact.
[14:44] Sarah: How do you validate quality in CI? We have clinical QA checks.
[14:49] Priya: Optimize integrates with eval sets — you can hook your CI to automatically run regression checks on every quant profile change and block rollouts if metrics degrade.
[15:03] [16:15] Elaine: On key management — can Redwood write to our KMS or only accept customer-managed keys?
[16:20] Avery: For Hosted we support customer-managed keys (bring-your-own-KMS) and for Private you'll fully control KMS/HSM. We'll share the KMS integration docs.
[16:32] Ravi: Any known cases where quantization changed tokenization or special tokens handling — like clinical markups?
[16:38] Diego: Not tokenization per se, but logits calibration can shift probability mass around special tokens; that's why we recommend calibration with your target tokens.
[16:50] [18:00] Avery: Quick demo of Console: showing per-route dashboard, latency histogram, cost breakdown, and a quant profile preview. The quant profile preview shows per-layer sensitivity and recommended precision.
[18:17] Priya: Note — the UI will suggest a "safe" profile and an "aggressive" profile; safe = more FP16 fallbacks, aggressive = more INT8. You can compare expected deltas before applying.
[18:32] Sarah: Are the predictions based on the exact model weights or on heuristics?
[18:36] Diego: We run a lightweight calibration pass on model weights and then extrapolate using your corpus; it's a mix of empirical and model-aware heuristics. Sometimes the transcribed doc here misses some nuance, but we'll share the exact methodology.
[18:52] [20:00] Ravi: How long does a calibration run take? For a 10k prompt set?
[20:05] Diego: On a single 48GB GPU it's approx 2–4 hours for 10k prompts depending on sequence length; we parallelize for dedicated clusters.
[20:17] Matt: Does this require downtime or can we run it live?
[20:21] Priya: It's non-blocking — you can run calibration in background, then schedule a maintenance window to apply profiles or use canary rollout.
[20:32] [22:00] Sarah: Ok next — benchmarking plan. We'll send 2k short notes + 500 long sequences. Can Redwood run a benchmark and provide logs?
[22:07] Avery: Yes — we'll run on Hosted and also simulate Dedicated latencies. We'll share raw latency histograms and cost estimates.
[22:19] Ravi: Please include P99 and tail latencies and also cache hit rates.
[22:24] Diego: Will do. Also we'll run FP16 baseline, FP8 profile, INT8 aggressive, and INT8 mixed.
[22:33] [24:00] Elaine: Last security question — can we get pen-test / attestation on model artifacts and the quantization pipeline?
[24:07] Avery: We can share SOC2 type II reports, and for private deployments we can enable further attestations. We'll add this to the security packet.
[24:20] Sarah: Great. Any blockers for us to start the pilot?
[24:25] Ravi: Only to gather prompts and to confirm masked vs real data path.
[24:30] Avery: Sounds good. We'll send the benchmark sheet and a short runbook for data handling.
[24:40] [25:00] Diego: One more note — quant profiles are versioned so you can always roll back. We also recommend keeping a small eval set in CI to catch regressions early.
[25:12] Priya: We'll include recommended thresholds for Rouge, F1, and hallucination metrics.
[25:22] [26:00] Sarah: Thanks — this was helpful. Next call to be the POC scoping where infra + security will join — can we do week of 4/27?
[26:10] Avery: Yes, we'll propose times.
[26:18] Ravi: Quick pricing Q — do you price quantized models differently?
[26:23] Priya: Pricing is primarily compute + reserved capacity tiers. Quantized models reduce compute cost which flows to lower usage charges; for Dedicated we can show committed pricing.
[26:36] Matt: How do you handle multi-tenant bursts if we go Dedicated?
[26:41] Diego: Dedicated gives you isolated pools; we still support autoscale and burst off a shared pool if you enable. That said, you can opt out for strict isolation.
[26:55] [28:00] Avery: Recap and next steps: we'll send benchmark spreadsheet, run a small 1k prompt pilot, provide security docs, and schedule the POC scoping.
[28:12] Sarah: Thanks all.
[28:20] Elaine: Bye.
